description.text: Danglars is the supercargo (the officer in charge of the cargo and accounts) of the Pharaon, about twenty-six years old. He fawns on his superiors, sneers at those below him, and is disliked by the crew. He resents Edmond Dantès, who is about to be made captain, and has been spying on him.

A cunning schemer who prefers to let others do his dirty work, Danglars gathers Dantès' rivals at La Réserve. He suggests prison as a way to part Dantès from Mercédès, and writes an anonymous denunciation with his left hand so that nothing can be traced back to him, then tosses it aside as a ‘joke’ within Fernand's reach.
After the arrest he fakes surprise, privately blames Fernand, and frightens Caderousse into silence. He also wins the trust of the shipowner Morrel.

Alone among the conspirators he sleeps peacefully: a cold calculator to whom a man's life matters less than a number. Fearing Dantès' revenge when Napoleon returns, he leaves the sea and goes to Madrid to work for a Spanish merchant.

In prison, the Abbé Faria helps Dantès work out that Danglars wrote the denunciation, disguising his hand. Dantès remembers, too, the inaccuracies in his accounts. He becomes one of the three men Dantès swears to punish.

According to Caderousse, Danglars became a cashier at a Spanish bank on Morrel's recommendation, made a fortune supplying the army, and married a second time, to a widow, Madame de Nargonne. He is now a millionaire baron living in the Rue du Mont-Blanc in Paris, and refused even to see the poor Caderousse.
Said to be worth six to eight million francs, he refused to help Morrel, the man to whom he owed the start of his fortune.
He is a baron ‘of a new creation’: Charles X gave him the title in 1829 for arranging a loan. He sits as an opposition deputy and plays the stock market, where he seems to get government news early.

Past fifty, with dyed black hair and a cunning face, he flaunts his wealth. He calls himself a man of the people but likes his servants to call him ‘my lord’. He suspects the Count's unlimited credit is a hoax, but is crushed by the Count's display of money. At home he sells his wife's favorite horses behind her back for profit.

Acting on false news, he panics and sells his Spanish bonds, losing about a million francs. Pale and surly afterwards, he is rude to his wife and eager to hear that the Cavalcanti are fabulously rich.

His marriage is a cold business arrangement. For sixteen years he has known of his wife's affairs, including her past with Villefort, and tolerated them for his own advantage; the couple have lived apart as husband and wife for four years. He cares only for his money.

His fortune is shakier than it looks: he has lost about 1,700,000 francs in a month. He now fancies the rich young Andrea Cavalcanti for Eugénie instead of Albert, resents the Morcerfs' older nobility, and reveals that the Count de Morcerf was once the fisherman Fernand Mondego. He writes at once to his correspondent in Yanina.

Cowardly but insolent, he puts off Morcerf's proposal for the marriage without explanation, then gloats over the newspaper paragraph about Yanina, saying it will make any explanation unnecessary. He gladly accepts Andrea as Eugénie's suitor once he hears of the young man's supposed millions, and promises a 500,000-franc dowry.
Challenged by Albert, he admits writing to Yanina, calls it a father's duty, and says the Count suggested it. He clearly has no intention of fighting.

In private he is a brutal husband and a domineering father. He admits to Eugénie that he is nearly ruined: he needs Andrea's three million, or at least the rumor of it, to cover a huge railway deposit, while he holds five and a half million belonging to charitable institutions that could be withdrawn at any time.
When soldiers burst in to arrest Andrea at the contract signing, Danglars shows abject terror, and is left humiliated and questioned by the police. By the end of the night his daughter has gone too.

Facing bankruptcy, he lets the Count walk off with the five million francs that belong to the charities in return for a receipt on Thomson & French of Rome. Telling the charities' Receiver-General to come back tomorrow, he gathers about 50,000 francs, burns some papers, writes to his wife and checks his passport.
He burns his papers and flees Paris by night, leaving his wife a mocking letter that accuses her of hiding away part of his fortune and leaves her ‘rich, but little respected’.

He reaches Rome and cashes the Count's receipt at Thomson & French, planning to collect his money in Venice and Vienna, unaware that the bandit Peppino is shadowing him. On the road out of Rome he is kidnapped and shut in Luigi Vampa's catacomb hideout. Since they have not killed him, he expects to be ransomed and still left rich.
Starved by his captors, who will sell him food only at ruinous prices (100,000 francs for a chicken), he soon has to sign drafts on his own fortune to eat.

Starved down to his last 50,000 francs, he prays for the first time in years and repents. His captor reveals himself as Edmond Dantès, the man he betrayed, and forgives him. Danglars is released with what little money he has left, and finds his hair has turned white.

description.text: A tall, dark-haired sailor of about nineteen, first mate of the merchant ship Pharaon. Skilled, calm and loved by the crew, he brings the ship home after Captain Leclere's death and is promised the captaincy by the owner, M. Morrel. He is devoted to his poor old father and engaged to the beautiful Mercédès.

Open and trusting, he offered his hand even to the hostile Fernand and invited Danglars, Caderousse and Fernand to his wedding. Arrested at the feast, he told the deputy prosecutor Villefort the whole truth about the letter he carried from Elba and trusted him as a friend, but was taken without trial to the Château d'If, where he swings between despair and rage.

Forgotten through the Hundred Days and after Waterloo, prisoner number 34 sank from prayer to rage to a decision to starve himself, until the sound of digging brought him back to life. His neighbour, the Abbé Faria, becomes his friend and teacher; together they work out that Danglars, Fernand and Villefort caused his ruin, and he swears vengeance. Gifted with a prodigious memory, he becomes a cultured man, and loyally refuses to escape without Faria.

Faria makes him heir to the lost Spada treasure, hidden on the island of Monte Cristo. When Faria dies, Dantès chooses life, revenge on his enemies and rewards for his friends, and boldly takes the dead man's place in his burial sack.

Now thirty-three, after exactly fourteen years in prison, he was rescued by smugglers, passing himself off as a Maltese sailor. Prison has made him pale, stern and unrecognisable, patient and secretive, though he grows fond of the loyal Jacopo. Following Faria's clues, he finds Cardinal Spada's treasure: an almost unimaginable fortune.
He returns to Marseilles unrecognised, travelling on an English passport as Lord Wilmore, and learns that his father is dead and Mercédès has vanished.

Disguised as an Italian priest, he hears from Caderousse exactly how he was betrayed and how his father starved. Then, posing as an English clerk of the bank Thomson & French, he takes Danglars's denunciation from the prison files and secretly rescues the ruined Morrel, signing himself “Sinbad the Sailor.” Having repaid kindness, he calls himself Heaven's substitute and sails off to punish the wicked.

As Sinbad he lives in a secret palace on Monte Cristo, friendly with smugglers and bandits. In Rome he is the Count of Monte Cristo, a figure of deathly pallor whom the bandit Vampa respects, and he reveals a cold philosophy of revenge: suffering inflicted over years must be repaid with suffering, not a quick death or a duel. He watches young Albert de Morcerf closely.

Learned, lavishly generous and cynical about gratitude, he rescues Albert from the bandits and asks him to introduce him to Paris, where 'plans long meditated' draw him. He arrives to the minute; Morrel's name moves him, and on meeting the Count and Countess of Morcerf he is paler even than Mercédès.

The Abbé Busoni who sent Bertuccio into his service was Dantès himself in disguise. He buys the Auteuil house tied to a dark secret of Villefort's, keeps the young Greek Haydée in secret apartments, and outplays Danglars with sheer wealth. To Villefort he calls himself one of the agents of Providence, rewarding and punishing.

With the grateful Morrels he almost gives himself away, crediting their rescue to an English friend, 'Lord Wilmore'. He leads Madame de Villefort on with talk of poisons, stages a fraud with a bogus 'Major Cavalcanti' and his 'son' Andrea, costs Danglars a fortune with a bribed telegraph operator, and at the Auteuil dinner torments Villefort and Madame Danglars with talk of a buried newborn child.

He prompts Danglars to look into what Fernand Mondego did at Yanina, and fools Villefort's police inquiry by playing both Busoni and Lord Wilmore. He refuses all food in Mercédès's house. As Busoni he catches Caderousse robbing his house and lets fate take its course, then whispers to the dying man his true name: Edmond Dantès.

Morcerf's treachery at Yanina is exposed, and Albert challenges the Count, who vows to kill him. Mercédès calls him Edmond and begs for her son; he promises Albert will live and resolves to die in the duel instead. Spared by Albert's apology, he reveals himself to Morcerf as Edmond Dantès, and begins to hope for happiness with Haydée.

He watched the poisonings in the Villefort house as God's justice, until he learned that Maximilian Morrel loves Valentine; from the house next door he now guards her night after night. He strips Danglars of five million francs, and stops Maximilian's suicide by revealing that he is Edmond Dantès, the man who saved his father.

He reveals to Villefort that Busoni and Monte Cristo are both Edmond Dantès, but the death of the child Edward makes him doubt his right to vengeance. He takes leave of Mercédès and revisits his cell in the Château d'If, where Faria's manuscript seems to confirm his mission.

He reveals himself to Danglars and pardons him. Hoping that saving Valentine and Morrel makes amends for the evil he has done, he gives them his property and sails away with Haydée, whose love he accepts as God's pardon.

description.text: Mercédès is Edmond Dantès’ fiancée, who lives in the Catalan village outside Marseille and has called on Morrel three times for news of his ship.
She is a beautiful seventeen-year-old with many admirers, often seen with a tall young cousin.

A poor orphan living on the village’s charity, she is honest and strong-willed. She loves her cousin Fernand only as a brother and has sworn that if Edmond dies, she will die too — a threat that keeps Fernand’s jealousy in check.
Radiant at the betrothal feast, she is heartbroken when Edmond is arrested and insists he is innocent.
Brave and dignified, she goes to Villefort herself to plead for Edmond, then spends the night numb with grief while Fernand watches over her.
Alone and desperate, she is kept from suicide only by her faith. She cares for Edmond’s father until he dies in her arms, and grows fonder of Fernand out of gratitude.
When Dantès returns to Marseille, she has vanished from the Catalan village.

Caderousse reveals that after eighteen months of waiting she married Fernand, in the very church where she was to have wed Edmond. She educated herself, has a son named Albert, and is now a rich countess in Paris, though Caderousse believes she is unhappy.

She is the Countess de Morcerf, mother of Albert. Her portrait shows her as a Catalan fisherwoman gazing at the sea, and she often weeps before it. Meeting the Count of Monte Cristo leaves her pale and shaken, and she questions Albert anxiously about him.
She quietly but firmly opposes Albert’s planned marriage to Eugénie Danglars, without explaining why, and keeps her distance from Madame Danglars.
The count fascinates and puzzles her; she talks of little else, imagines him a Cagliostro, and begs Albert to make sure he comes to her summer ball.
At her summer ball she watches him closely and notices that he will not eat or drink anything under her husband’s roof — and she understands it as deliberate.
She pleads with him to share food with her as a sign of friendship and asks searching questions about his past, but he refuses even a grape.
After her husband’s disgrace she is bedridden with shame. When Albert calls the count an enemy she turns pale and begs him to remain his friend, then has her son followed, fearing what he will do.

She recognized Edmond by his voice from the first moment. Coming to him secretly at night, she blames herself for marrying Fernand, admits she still loves him, and learns only now why he was arrested. She begs him to spare Albert’s life.
By telling Albert the family secret, she saves both her son and the count from the duel.
She leaves her husband’s house taking nothing, urges Albert to take her father’s name, Herrera, and accepts the small treasure Edmond buried for her as a dowry for a convent.
She and Albert give their whole fortune to the hospitals.
Living in a bare, cold room, she has lost her sparkle but not her dignity. She agrees to go to Marseille, to the little house where Edmond’s money waits for her.
Living in old Dantès’ house, she blames herself rather than Edmond: she was weak and married Fernand. She asks only for Albert’s happiness and means to spend her life in prayer.

description.text: M. Morrel owns the Marseille shipping firm Morrel & Son and its ship the Pharaon. He is kind, fair and fond of young Dantès, whom he plans to make captain. He seems to have a quiet sympathy for Napoleon, in whose army his uncle Policar served.

He honours Dantès' betrothal feast with his presence and, when Edmond is arrested, rushes to help. Convinced of his innocence, he goes to plead with the deputy prosecutor Villefort, and meanwhile gives Danglars temporary command of the Pharaon.
Villefort receives him coldly, treating him as a suspected Bonapartist. Morrel goes on to appeal to every influential friend he has, and is refused everywhere.

During Napoleon's brief return to power he petitions again and again for Dantès' release, never suspecting that Villefort is deceiving him. Cautious but loyal, he pays for old Dantès' funeral even though helping a 'Bonapartist' family is dangerous.

Years later, Caderousse describes how Morrel was persecuted as a Bonapartist for his petitions. Now he has lost five ships and is close to ruin, with only the Pharaon left to save him. He has a wife, a daughter, and a son who is an army lieutenant.

He has told his creditors he cannot pay unless the Pharaon arrives by the 15th. The prison files show that his 1815 petition for Dantès was later used by Villefort as proof that Dantès was a dangerous Bonapartist.

Aged by fourteen years of trouble, he is still scrupulously honest and proud that his firm has never failed to honour a signature. Then news comes that the Pharaon has sunk, leaving him 287,500 francs in debt and nothing to pay with; he thanks God that the crew survived.

Believing a suicide leaves an honest name where bankruptcy would not, and refused help by Danglars, he prepares to shoot himself. At the stroke of eleven he is saved by a purse sent by 'Sinbad the Sailor' holding his settled debt, and a brand-new Pharaon sails into port. The reader knows the mysterious Englishman and 'Sinbad' were Edmond Dantès repaying his old patron; Morrel does not.
He has since died, leaving his children comfortably off. He always insisted 'It was no Englishman that thus saved us', and his last words were 'Maximilian, it was Edmond Dantès!'
Maximilian recalls that his father was wholly devoted to the emperor, just as Villefort was to the Bourbons.
The Count finally tells Maximilian that he was the one who saved his father from suicide, ten years ago to the day, on 5 September.
He died in his children's arms and lies in Marseille beside his wife, who died two years before him.

description.text: Caderousse is old Dantès' neighbour, a bearded tailor of about twenty-five. Friendly on the surface, he is envious and greedy underneath and resents Edmond's good fortune, and he runs straight to Danglars with news of Mercédès' Catalan ‘cousin’.
At La Réserve he drinks heavily and taunts Fernand. Drunk but not blind, he protests that Dantès is his friend and calls the denunciation an infamous shame, but he is easily steered by Danglars.
Sober, he remembers the letter and wants to tell the truth, but fear of being called an accomplice wins out. Unable either to act or to forget, he tries to drown his guilt in brandy.

Years later he has fallen on hard times and keeps a poor inn on the road between Bellegarde and Beaucaire with his sickly wife, La Carconte. Vain, envious and loud about his own honesty, he seems truly sorry about Dantès, but the sight of a diamond loosens his tongue.

He admits he was present, drunk, when the denunciation was written, and says remorse haunts him. He tells the abbé the whole story of the betrayal and how Danglars and Fernand rose, and receives the diamond as his reward.

He sells the diamond to a jeweller for 45,000 francs. Egged on by his wife, he stabs the jeweller to death in the night and flees with the money and the diamond. Caught abroad, he confesses and is sent to the galleys for life.
Now a ragged, wolfish figure, he has slipped away from the prison at Toulon and is hiding in Paris. He knows Andrea Cavalcanti's real name, Benedetto, and his past, and means to live off him.

Living on the Rue Ménilmontant as a ‘retired baker’ on Andrea's money, he turns out to be Andrea's old galley comrade, with whom he escaped from Toulon. Greedy and resentful, he extorts more, takes Andrea's diamond, and studies a plan of the Count's house.

He breaks into the Count's house and is caught by the Abbé Busoni, to whom he insists La Carconte was the jeweller's real murderer. When the abbé threatens to expose him, he tries to stab him. Climbing back over the wall, he is stabbed three times by an accomplice.
Dying, he names Benedetto as his murderer and signs a deposition. He denies God until the Count whispers his real name, Edmond Dantès; then he begs God's pardon and dies.
His missing waistcoat turns up with a bloodstained letter to Danglars in the pocket, which exposes Andrea at the contract signing.
His dying accusation is the key evidence against Benedetto.

Agreed to ‘wait and see’ rather than speak up for Dantès.
Told the abbé that old Dantès died of starvation.
Told the abbé who had denounced Dantès and received the diamond.

Named Benedetto as his murderer and died repenting.

tagline.text: Mercédès’ tall, fierce Catalan cousin, jealous of her love for Dantès.
Mercédès’ jealous cousin, who carried off Danglars’ denunciation of Dantès.
Mercédès’ cousin, one of the men who sent Dantès to prison.
Dantès’ betrayer, now the Count de Morcerf, a rich general married to Mercédès.
The Count de Morcerf, Albert’s father: a general and peer of France.
The Count de Morcerf, publicly accused of betraying Ali Pasha at Yanina.
The Count de Morcerf, convicted of treason by the Chamber of Peers.
The disgraced Count de Morcerf, abandoned by his wife and son.

description.text: Caderousse describes a strapping, fierce-looking young Catalan of about twenty-one who escorts Mercédès and seems to be courting her. Fernand is Mercédès’ cousin, a Catalan fisherman who has loved her for ten years. Jealous and quick to reach for his knife, he is held back only by her vow to die if Edmond is harmed.
He openly admits he hates Dantès and will do anything short of killing him. When Danglars writes an anonymous denunciation and throws it aside, Fernand secretly picks it up.
Pale and tense through the betrothal feast, he slips away just before the arrest and then returns to act as Mercédès’ protector.
He stays at Mercédès’ side through her grief, brooding over Dantès, until he is called up into Napoleon’s army. Her farewell gives him hope.
In prison, Dantès works out that Fernand was Danglars’ partner in the plot, driven by his love for Mercédès.

Caderousse reveals that Fernand posted the letter. Drafted in 1815, he deserted to the enemy with his general, rose under the restored king, and became a count after the Spanish war. As the Count de Morcerf he served Ali Pasha in Greece, came home rich, and is now a lieutenant-general living in Paris, married to Mercédès.

Albert’s father is a general and peer of France who looks older than his forty-odd years, with white hair and a careworn face. He dislikes his wife’s Catalan portrait, and is easily charmed by the Count of Monte Cristo’s flattery.

At the Opera he confirms he was inspector-general of Ali Pasha’s troops at Yanina and owes his fortune to the pasha’s generosity. He seems unsettled to hear that the Count’s companion is Greek — and she, seeing him, accuses him of selling her father to the Turks.
He is eager for Albert to marry Eugénie Danglars.
Danglars sneers that the count began life as a fisherman named Fernand Mondego, and mentions unpleasant rumours from Greece about Ali Pasha. Danglars writes to Yanina to find out more.

Proud and irritable, he formally asks for Eugénie’s hand for Albert, but Danglars stalls with hints of slander. A newspaper then claims that the castle of Yanina was betrayed to the Turks by a French officer named Fernand.
Beauchamp’s inquiries in Yanina prove that Colonel Fernand Mondego, raised by Ali to high command, surrendered the castle for two million crowns — and that he is the Count de Morcerf.

Named openly in the press, he defends himself before the Chamber of Peers, claiming he was negotiating for Ali when the pasha died. Haydée appears as a witness, accuses him of the false pardon, of stabbing Selim and of selling her and her mother as slaves, and produces the bill of sale. Speechless, he is convicted of treason.
The count tells Mercédès that Fernand posted the denunciation Danglars wrote, and lists his later betrayals: in Spain, against Ali, and against France itself.

Believing Albert has avenged him, then learning of the apology, he goes to fight Monte Cristo to the death. When the count reveals himself as Edmond Dantès, Fernand flees home, watches his wife and son leave him, and shoots himself.

tagline.text: The ambitious royalist deputy prosecutor handling Dantès' case in Marseilles.
Ambitious deputy prosecutor who buried an innocent Dantès in prison to protect his career.
Rising royalist magistrate, married to Renée, who kept Dantès locked away.
An 'upright' magistrate whom Bertuccio accuses of burying a child at Auteuil.
Cold, powerful king's attorney in Paris, Valentine's father and Noirtier's son.
Paris prosecutor haunted by his buried child and terrified Monte Cristo knows his secret.
King's attorney hushing up a suspected poisoning in his own household.
Prosecutor who has unmasked his own wife as the household poisoner.

description.text: The deputy prosecutor in Marseilles who takes charge of Dantès' case. He is known as a fierce royalist and an ambitious young man.

Young, eloquent and proud of the death sentences he wins, Villefort has given up his father's name and politics to get ahead. He is engaged to Renée de Saint-Méran, daughter of a royalist family, and leaves his own betrothal feast to examine the prisoner.

Gérard de Villefort is twenty-seven, rich, and practises his serious face in the mirror. He sees that Dantès is innocent, but the letter Dantès carried is addressed to his own Bonapartist father, Noirtier. To save his career he burns it, makes Dantès promise silence, and quietly arranges for him to stay locked up.
Sensing a political storm, he rushes to Paris to win the king's gratitude. He coldly turns away Mercédès, and feels his first pang of remorse, but ambition wins.

He warns Louis XVIII of Napoleon's escape from Elba, hiding his father's role, and is rewarded with the king's own cross of the Legion of Honour. Then a stranger matching the police description of the suspect in General Quesnel's death walks into his hotel room: his father, Noirtier.

Father and son, on opposite sides, protect each other: Villefort warns Noirtier of the police description, Noirtier disguises himself in his son's clothes and promises to shield him in return, and Villefort hurries back to Marseilles.

He survives Napoleon's return thanks to his father's protection, holds back Morrel's petitions, and makes sure Dantès stays buried. After Waterloo he marries Renée and becomes king's attorney at Toulouse.
Dantès' prison file shows his handiwork: a note in Villefort's writing brands Dantès an inveterate Bonapartist to be kept in strict solitary confinement.

Years later, he has the reputation of the most upright of magistrates, having served as king's attorney at Nîmes and Versailles. But Bertuccio, recognizing the Auteuil garden, calls him a villain and says he once buried a child there.

Bertuccio's story: in 1815 Villefort coldly refused him justice for his murdered brother. Later, at his father-in-law's house in Auteuil, Villefort secretly visited a pregnant young woman known as 'the Baroness', and one night buried a newborn in a box in the garden. Bertuccio stabbed him there, then dug up the box and found the baby still alive.

Villefort survived the stabbing and is now an important king's attorney in Paris, having kept his post through four revolutions. Thin, sallow, cold and rigidly correct, he is feared rather than liked. He lives with his second wife Héloïse, his daughter Valentine, his son Edward, and his paralyzed father, whose condition he believes is God's punishment for some fault unknown to human justice.

He is determined to marry Valentine to Franz d'Épinay, and treats his father's furious opposition as an old man's whim. He visits Noirtier rarely and coldly, and darkly hints that the old man knows something about the murder of Franz's father.

At the Count's dinner at Auteuil his hand trembles as he arrives, and Bertuccio recognizes him as the man he stabbed in that very garden. The pregnant woman of the story was Madame Danglars, and the baby Bertuccio saved grew up to be Benedetto, now passing as Andrea Cavalcanti.

Alone with Madame Danglars he tells his side: he believed the baby stillborn and buried it himself, was stabbed by a Corsican, and a year later found the grave empty. He traced the child to a foundling hospital and lost the trail. Convinced Monte Cristo knows his secret, he vows to find out who the Count really is.
Posing as an envoy of the prefect of police, he questions the Abbé Busoni and Lord Wilmore about the Count, without learning anything that alarms him.
When Madame de Saint-Méran dies and Dr. d'Avrigny suspects poison, Villefort's first concern is to avoid scandal and keep his enemies from triumphing. He persuades the doctor to say nothing.
Citing the marquise's dying wish, he rushes Franz into signing Valentine's marriage contract straight from the funeral.
Noirtier reveals to Franz that he killed Franz's father in a duel. Villefort flees the room, tempted to smother what life remains in the old man.
Franz's harsh letter breaking off the engagement wounds Villefort's pride; he had always believed the general was assassinated, not killed in a fair duel.
After Barrois is poisoned, d'Avrigny accuses Valentine. Villefort admits a crime has been committed but begs on his knees not to give his daughter up to justice.

His household lives in terror, and he admits the deaths may not have been natural. He tells the Count that condemning criminals reassures him he is not uniquely wicked, and swears before a crucifix that the culprits in his house will die, whoever they are.
When Valentine is found dead, the 'iron heart' of Villefort is overwhelmed by real grief for the first time.
Noirtier tells him privately who the murderer is. Villefort begs that the family's honour be protected and swears to take terrible revenge within three days.

He has known since Madame de Saint-Méran's death that a poisoner lived in his house, and after Valentine's death he no longer doubted it was his wife. To save his name from the scaffold, he orders Héloïse to take her own poison before he comes back from court.
At Benedetto's trial, the accused names the king's attorney as his father. Villefort admits everything, says he is in the hands of an avenging God, and leaves the court a ruined man.

Humbled, he rushes home resolved to save his wife and flee with her, but finds her and Edward dead. When the Count reveals he is Edmond Dantès, Villefort loses his reason and begins digging in the garden for his lost child.

The witty Bourbon king, caught off guard by Napoleon's return from Elba.

description.text: The restored Bourbon king, toasted by the royalists of Marseilles, who reportedly approves of Villefort's marriage.
A witty, scholarly king who annotates Horace and laughs off warnings. He knows who Villefort's father is but values the son's zeal.
Humiliated to learn of Napoleon's landing only by telegraph, he turns bitterly on his ministers and rewards Villefort with his own cross of the Legion of Honour.
He flees during the Hundred Days and is restored after Waterloo.

description.text: An old royalist nobleman, father of Villefort's fiancée Renée, who toasts Louis XVIII and wants the family's political quarrels forgotten.
On Villefort's advice he sells his bonds and arranges the letter that gets Villefort an audience with the king.
After the Restoration he stands higher at court than ever.
He owned the house at Auteuil, which was said to have been rented to a young widow known as 'the Baroness'. He has since sold it, to the Count.
He is Valentine's grandfather on her mother's side, and she is the sole heiress of him and his wife.
News reaches Paris that he has died on the road from Marseilles while travelling to hasten Valentine's marriage.
His widow tells how, unwell but determined to see Valentine, he took his usual lozenges, fell into an unnaturally deep sleep, cried out and died. A doctor called it apoplexy.
After two more deaths in the household, Dr. d'Avrigny becomes convinced from his symptoms that he too was poisoned.

tagline.text: Renée's stern, fiercely royalist mother.
Valentine's proud grandmother, just arrived in Paris with news of her husband's death.

Valentine's grandmother, who died suddenly days after her husband.

description.text: Renée's stern, fiercely royalist mother. She keeps reminding Villefort of his father's revolutionary past and urges him to be merciless to conspirators.
She is Valentine's grandmother, and Valentine expects to inherit from her.

She arrives in Paris with the news of her husband's death. Proud and contemptuous of anyone not noble, she adores Valentine, resents Villefort's remarriage, and, feverish and sure she will die soon, demands the wedding to Franz at once. She describes a white figure that entered her room at night and touched her glass.
She dies after three violent convulsive attacks, her last wish being that Valentine's marriage not be delayed. Dr. d'Avrigny privately tells Villefort she was poisoned, but agrees to keep quiet.
She was sixty-six. Her will leaves the whole Saint-Méran fortune to Valentine, and society blames her death on grief.

moments.text: Described a white figure touching her glass at night, then drank her orangeade and demanded a notary.
Died after three violent convulsive attacks.

Villefort's Bonapartist father, to whom Dantès' Elba letter was addressed.

description.text: Villefort's father, mentioned at the royalist betrothal feast as a former Girondin revolutionary who became a senator under Napoleon and is perhaps still a Bonapartist. His son has dropped his name to escape his politics.
The letter Dantès carried from Elba was addressed to M. Noirtier, Rue Coq-Héron, Paris. That is why Villefort destroys it: the link to his father could ruin him.

He matches the police description of the man who lured the royalist General Quesnel to a Bonapartist club shortly before the general was found dead. Without warning, he walks into his son's hotel room calling him 'my dear Gérard'.

Witty, well informed and utterly fearless, he is vice-president of the Bonapartist club of the Rue Saint-Jacques and believes that in politics there are no murders, only obstacles removed. He shaves off his whiskers, puts on his son's clothes, and strolls past the police.
Powerful at Napoleon's court during the Hundred Days, he protects his son's position in return.
Years later he is paralyzed by a stroke and unable to speak, entirely dependent on his granddaughter Valentine. He was once a fiery Jacobin, senator and conspirator famous across Europe.
His mind is fully alert. He speaks with his eyes, and only Valentine can read them. He is the one person at home who truly loves her.

He signals yes by closing his eyes and no by blinking, and his will is as strong as ever. He detests the plan to marry Valentine to Franz d'Épinay; there was once a bitter political hatred between him and Franz's father, and Villefort hints that Noirtier knows something about that man's murder.

With Valentine as interpreter, he dictates a will leaving his fortune of 900,000 francs to the poor if she marries Franz. He refuses, with something like hatred, to leave anything to his son or grandson Edward.
He approves of Maximilian Morrel, but forbids an elopement or a duel, insisting that help will come from him alone.

He stops the contract by showing Franz a signed record of 5 February 1815: as president of the Bonapartist club, Noirtier killed Franz's father, General d'Épinay, in a fair duel, and was wounded three times doing it. When Franz asks who killed his father, Noirtier spells out 'myself'.
At Madame de Villefort's request, he makes a new will leaving everything to Valentine, on condition she never leaves him.

His servant Barrois dies after drinking Noirtier's lemonade. D'Avrigny believes the poison was meant for Noirtier himself, who survived only because a year of brucine treatment had accustomed his body to it.

He has been quietly protecting Valentine by dosing her with his own medicine, building up her resistance. When she collapses, he confirms to d'Avrigny that the hand that killed Barrois struck her too.
The Count believes Noirtier knows, or at least suspects, who the poisoner is.
After Valentine's death, he tells Villefort privately who the murderer is, and agrees to keep it secret because his son has sworn revenge.
After a night in which the Abbé Busoni watches over Valentine's body, Noirtier sleeps calmly, almost smiling, to everyone's surprise.
Ever since the abbé's vigil he has been calm and resigned. In the garden he glares with hatred at Madame de Villefort, then at his son, silently reminding him of his oath.
He is waiting at Leghorn to bless Valentine before her marriage to Morrel.

He was found in the Seine the day after leaving home. Noirtier tells his son the general heard the club's plans, declared himself a royalist, reluctantly swore an oath, and 'lost his way' on leaving. His words strongly suggest the general was killed.

Dantès's fellow prisoner, friend and teacher, who uncovers the plot against him.
Dantès's teacher, who reveals that the Spada treasure is real and makes him his heir.
Dantès's beloved teacher, who died in the Château d'If and left him the Spada treasure.

description.text: An Italian priest born in Rome, for twenty years secretary to Cardinal Spada, arrested at Piombino in 1811 for dreaming of a united Italy. Everyone thinks he is mad because he keeps offering a huge treasure in exchange for his freedom.
Cautious and patient, he has dug a long tunnel hoping to reach the sea, but miscalculated and broke into Dantès's cell instead. He says he is alone in the world.
A small, agile man of about sixty: a scholar, chemist and linguist who refuses to shed blood. In prison he has made his own tools, pens, ink and linen 'paper', and written a book on Italian monarchy.

A brilliant reasoner, he works out who betrayed Dantès and why, and becomes his patient teacher in languages, science and the ways of the world. He suffers from an inherited catalepsy that killed his father and grandfather on a third attack; a second attack leaves him partly paralysed.

He was never mad: as secretary to the last Count of Spada he inherited the family papers and, in 1807, found Cardinal Spada's hidden letter revealing a treasure on Monte Cristo. He makes Dantès his heir, calling him 'the child of my captivity'.
He spends his last months making Dantès memorise the treasure letter and dies selflessly, refusing to let him call for help. His homemade knife, needle and thread make Dantès's escape possible.
Everything he taught proves right: his clues lead Dantès to the treasure, and everything he deduced about Dantès's betrayers is confirmed.

description.text: A rich Roman noble made a cardinal in 1498, then poisoned at dinner by Pope Alexander VI and Cæsar Borgia. He had foreseen the trap and hid his fortune in the caves of Monte Cristo for his nephew Guido, leaving a secret letter in invisible ink.
He hid the treasure with great cunning: marks carved in the rocks as a guide, a boulder slid into place, a false wall painted like granite, and a buried chest bearing the Spada arms.

tagline.text: Son of Pope Alexander VI, who poisoned Cardinal Spada for his wealth.

description.text: Son of Pope Alexander VI. He and his father poisoned rich cardinals to seize their wealth, but they never found Cardinal Spada's fortune.

description.text: The last of the Spada family and Faria's patron. Poor despite the family legend of hidden wealth, he left Faria his library and the famous breviary in which the treasure letter was hidden.

Master of La Jeune Amélie, named as Captain Baldi: a shrewd smuggler well known to the coast guards and fluent in many languages. He trusts Dantès, sees him as his natural successor and delays sailing out of concern for him.

A Corsican devoted to Edmond: he nurses him when he is wounded, indignantly refuses payment, and learns navigation and astronomy from him.
Loyal as ever, he offers to give up his share of the profits to stay and nurse Dantès on Monte Cristo.
Rewarded with a boat of his own, he believes the story of Dantès's inheritance and serves him loyally as a messenger.

description.text: La Carconte is Caderousse's wife, born near Arles and once beautiful, now wasted by fever. Bitter and suspicious, she urges her husband to keep quiet because Fernand and Danglars are powerful enough to crush them, and doubts that the abbé's diamond is real.

Greedy as well as feverish, she pushes Caderousse to sell the diamond, then plans the murder of the jeweller. She is shot dead on the stairs in the struggle; Caderousse later insists she was the real killer.

description.text: Caderousse mentions little Albert, the son of Mercédès and Fernand, whom Mercédès was educating herself during the Spanish war.

The Viscount Albert de Morcerf is a young man of Paris high society travelling to Rome for the Carnival with his friend Franz. Morcerf is the title Caderousse said Fernand now holds — and Mercédès’ son was named Albert.
Breezy and self-assured, he believes a full purse can do anything, and he is brave to the point of recklessness, laughing off the bandit Vampa as a myth.
He is vain about his clothes and stung by his lack of romantic success in Italy, but also talented and well off, with a comfortable income. He knows some Greek.
Kidnapped by Vampa’s bandits, he shows remarkable coolness, sleeping soundly under threat of death. Freed by the Count of Monte Cristo, he feels eternally in his debt.
Grateful and carefree, he offers the Count his family’s influence in Paris and brushes off all of Franz’s suspicions. His father, the Count de Morcerf, has called him home to arrange a marriage.
He lives a pampered life in a pavilion in his parents’ courtyard, full of half-abandoned hobbies and a dandy’s pursuits.
Paris gossip links him to Eugénie Danglars, daughter of the newly made Baron Danglars, a match his father is most anxious for.
His mother is the Countess de Morcerf — Mercédès. He believes his parents have been happily married for over twenty years, their only disagreement being her portrait.
Not yet twenty-one, he does not want to marry Eugénie. Torn between his father’s wishes and his mother’s unhappiness, he would rather displease his father, and has stalled the marriage talks.
He adores his mother — what he really wants is a wife like her — and dreads marrying Eugénie.
At his parents’ ball he is a witty guide to the guests, and presses the count to eat at his mother’s request without understanding why it matters to her.
He knows his father made his fortune serving Ali Pasha. Visiting the count, he is enchanted by Haydée and hears her story of her father’s betrayal.
When a newspaper claims Yanina was betrayed by an officer named Fernand, he furiously takes it as a slander on his father and challenges Beauchamp, the editor, to a duel.

Beauchamp returns from Yanina with proof that his father really did betray the castle. Albert burns the proofs, grieves for his father and fears for his mother. His engagement to Eugénie is broken off.
Wanting a living enemy to fight, he works out that Monte Cristo planned every step of his father’s exposure.
Suspecting his mother of special reasons for defending the count, he insults Monte Cristo publicly at the Opera, leading to a duel.
After a sleepless night he apologizes on the dueling ground, saying the count had the right to avenge himself — not for Ali’s sake, but for the fisherman Fernand’s treachery toward him.
His friends receive the apology coldly. He gives up his luxuries, his father’s name and his fortune, and leaves home with his mother, planning to earn his own living.
He has sold his watch and enlisted in the Spahis, a cavalry regiment in Africa, to make a name of his own and support his mother.
Now in uniform, he sails from Marseille to Algiers.

description.text: Caderousse says Fernand served Ali Pasha in Greece as instructor-general, and that before Ali was killed he rewarded Fernand with a large sum of money.
Ali Tepelini, the Albanian chief of Yanina, had Morcerf as inspector-general of his troops, and Morcerf admits he owes his fortune to him. Haydée’s furious outburst suggests Ali was her father.

Haydée reveals he was her father. Waiting for the sultan’s verdict, he retreated to a fortified kiosk on a lake, with his gold and gunpowder guarded by the faithful Selim, and sent a French officer he trusted to negotiate. A false pardon tricked the guard into putting out the match, and Ali was killed by the sultan’s troops.
Before the Chamber of Peers, Morcerf produces Ali’s letters and ring, but Haydée declares that Morcerf himself brought back the false pardon.

moments.text: Was betrayed by the false pardon and killed by the sultan’s soldiers.

description.text: Inspector of prisons for fourteen years, he had invested his daughter's dowry of two hundred thousand francs with Morrel and was in despair. He believes the prisoner Dantès drowned while escaping and finds the story funny. He sells his doubtful claim at full value to the Englishman from Thomson & French and lets him search the prison registers.
Now risen to a high post in the police, he handles Villefort's request for information about the Count of Monte Cristo.
Now Receiver-General of the charities, he comes to Danglars for five million francs owed to the hospitals. He does not recognise the Count, who bows to him as if they had met before.

description.text: A young clerk of twenty-three or twenty-four who stays with Morrel's failing firm because he loves Morrel's daughter Julie.
Julie trusts him above everyone: he urges her to obey the Sinbad letter, escorts her on her errand, and brings the news of the new Pharaon.
Now about thirty, he is Julie's husband, honoured for having stayed loyal to the Morrels when their fortunes fell.
He ran the family firm until he had earned 250,000 francs to match his wife's inheritance, then closed the business rather than sell the Morrel name. He finds the Count a strange man.
At Maximilian's request he agrees to serve as the Count's second witness at the meeting with Albert de Morcerf.
When the affair ends peacefully he does not hide his joy and hurries home to Julie.
When the Count reveals himself as the family's benefactor, Emmanuel gently reproaches him for hiding so long. The Count asks him to watch over Maximilian.
He believes the falls of Morcerf, Danglars and Villefort were directed by Providence, and calls the Count an angel.

description.text: Morrel's beautiful daughter, sixteen or seventeen and devoted to her father. She blushes when a stranger from Thomson & French hints that she will marry the clerk Emmanuel, and she promises to obey a letter signed 'Sinbad the Sailor'.
Trusting the letter despite her fears, she fetches a red silk purse from the Allées de Meilhan and reaches her father just in time to save him.
Nearly nine years on she is twenty-five, married to Emmanuel Herbaut and, as her brother says, 'as happy as it is permitted to a human creature to be'. She lives in the Rue Meslay in Paris.
She longs to thank the family's unknown benefactor and keeps his purse, letter and diamond as treasured relics, which she shows the visiting Count. She feels she has heard his voice before.
When she learns that the Count is the benefactor, she brings out the purse from under its crystal globe to honour him and refuses to give it back.
Sensing her brother is hiding something, she begs the Count to restore his happiness. She still trusts 'Sinbad the Sailor'.

description.text: Morrel's son, about twenty-two, trained at the Polytechnic School and now a sub-lieutenant in the 53rd infantry. His strict sense of duty has earned him the nickname 'the stoic', and he has great influence over his father. Told of the family's ruin, he heartbrokenly accepts his father's choice to die and swears to live on and restore the family name, before the mysterious rescue saves them all.

Years later he is a captain of Spahis (French cavalry in Algeria) and a member of the Legion of Honour, dignified and brave; he once saved Château-Renaud from Arab horsemen. Every 5 September, the anniversary of his father's rescue, he tries to do some good deed, and he is still hunting for the unknown benefactor who acted through Thomson & French. His sister is happily married to Emmanuel Herbaut. The reader knows that benefactor was Dantès.

When the Count calls at the family home in the Rue Meslay, Maximilian is warm and open. He tells how Julie and Emmanuel wound up the firm with honour, and that his father died convinced their rescuer was Edmond Dantès. He feels the Count 'likes us'.

He is secretly and passionately in love with Valentine de Villefort, who is engaged to Franz d'Épinay. He has rented the plot behind her garden and poses as a gardener so they can talk through a boarded gate, and he scrupulously respects every limit she sets, hoping Providence will free her.
He feels a mysterious bond with Monte Cristo and half believes the Count quietly arranges good fortune for him. He keeps his love for Valentine secret even from his sister.

Now thirty, he is in despair as Valentine's marriage to Franz is hurried forward, and resolves to kill himself if it goes ahead. Hiding in the garden, he overhears Dr. d'Avrigny tell Villefort that Madame de Saint-Méran was poisoned, but says nothing to Valentine. Brought before Noirtier, he swears to wait for the old man's decision.
When Noirtier's revelation breaks off the engagement to Franz, Valentine tells Maximilian at the gate that they are saved, and he comes to worship the old man.
Visiting the Villefort house, he witnesses the servant Barrois' collapse and slips away unseen.
At the Opera he stops Albert de Morcerf from throwing his glove at the Count, then agrees to act as the Count's second, chilled by how coldly the Count speaks of killing Albert.

On the morning of the duel the Count sends his will to the solicitor, telling Maximilian to examine it if he dies. Maximilian admits he loves a young girl more than his life, secures the first shot for his friend, and begs him to spare Albert.
Riding back from the duel, the Count reminds him that he has great power and will gladly use it for those he loves.
Now allowed to visit Valentine twice a week, he has learned to read Noirtier's signals, and he is present when Valentine collapses.
In his fear he tells Monte Cristo what he overheard about poison and confesses that he loves Valentine de Villefort.
Trusting the Count's promise, he is caught off guard when he finds the house deserted, and rushes upstairs to hear that Valentine is dead.
He carries Noirtier up to her deathbed, declares himself her betrothed, denounces her murder, and blames himself for never revealing what he overheard.

He meant to shoot himself after the funeral; he had never loved anyone before he met Valentine at twenty-nine. The Count stops him, revealing that he is Edmond Dantès, the man who saved his father, and makes him swear to wait one month, until 5 October.
Numb and hopeless, he follows the Count to Marseille and weeps at his father's grave, feeling that leaving Paris is like losing Valentine a second time.
He renews his promise to wait and agrees to be brought from Bastia to the island of Monte Cristo on 5 October.

Having waited a month in vain, he comes calmly to die, refusing even the Count's fortune, and swallows what he believes is a fatal drug. He wakes to find Valentine alive beside him; the Count's farewell gifts go to him as the son of his old master.

description.text: A mute Nubian servant of Franz's mysterious host on Monte Cristo. The Bey of Tunis had his tongue cut out and was about to take his hand and head when 'Sinbad' bought his life with a fine gun and a cutlass, and Ali is utterly devoted to him.
In Rome, Franz recognizes the Count's driver as the mute servant from the grotto on Monte Cristo.
Sent a week ahead to Paris, he buys and furnishes a house for the Count and meets him at the city gate with the address.
He chose the house on the Champs-Élysées and greets his master with sincere joy.
The Count calls him a slave whose life belongs to him, and Ali happily agrees, though the Count is unexpectedly gentle with him.
A skilled lasso thrower who says he has hunted lions, he stops Madame de Villefort's runaway carriage single-handed and calms the horses completely.
He is to escort Haydée whenever she goes out, and is amazed to see his usually stern master happy.
He serves as the Count's silent, trusted aide: on the night of the burglary he keeps watch at his side with a hatchet and brings him the abbé's disguise.
He drives the Count's carriage on the road to Normandy at breathtaking speed, in his element like a 'child of the desert'.
He brings the Count his pistols on the eve of the duel.
On the morning of the duel he carries the Count's sealed will to the solicitor.
He goes ahead with Haydée when the Count leaves Paris.
He carries a letter from the Count to Noirtier and mimes the old man's 'yes' in reply.

description.text: Baron Franz d’Épinay is a young Parisian aristocrat who has lived in Italy for years and guides Albert there. Cool in danger but very curious, he dines with a mysterious host calling himself Sinbad on the island of Monte Cristo, and senses a man thirsting for revenge.
In Rome he pieces the clues together and realizes Sinbad is the Count of Monte Cristo. He admires the count but is repelled by his ideas and wary of him.
Loyal and quick-witted, he turns to the count to rescue the kidnapped Albert. Afterwards he tells Albert all he has seen, but Albert dismisses his suspicions.
He is Valentine de Villefort’s fiancé, a match her father insists on.
His mother died at his birth and his father, General de Quesnel, Baron d’Épinay, was assassinated in 1815 when Franz was two, supposedly by Bonapartists.
Honourable and sincere, he keeps his word to marry Valentine despite her lost inheritance, saying he seeks happiness, not money.
Summoned by Noirtier, he learns at last the truth about his father’s death: Noirtier killed him in a duel.
Shaken, he formally breaks off the engagement, writing that Villefort should have told him first. Albert names him as one of the seconds he wants in his quarrel with Beauchamp.
At Albert’s request he attends the duel with Monte Cristo, and is bewildered when Albert apologizes.

An obsequious but practical innkeeper, he warns that no carriages can be had at Carnival time. The rest of his floor is let to a mysterious rich traveller.
He knew the bandit Luigi Vampa as a child, and was once captured and released by him, receiving a fine Bréguet watch. He tells the friends Vampa's story.
He arranges his neighbour the Count's offer of carriage seats and windows, and collects execution notices for his guests' convenience.
He conjures up ready-made peasant costumes for the friends' Carnival outing.
Alarmed by a messenger who arrives at night, he arranges Franz's late audience with the Count.
Years later he welcomes Danglars to his hotel and interprets for him.

description.text: A famous bandit of about twenty-two, once a shepherd of remarkable intelligence, pride and marksmanship. Moody and jealous, he burned the San-Felice villa to win his beloved Teresa a fine costume, then shot the brutal chief Cucumetto and took over his band. He kills prisoners whose ransom arrives late, and hides among shepherds, fishermen and islands such as Monte Cristo.

He pays an informer inside the papal prison and is fiercely loyal to those who serve him. At the Colosseum Franz overhears him pledge total obedience to a cloaked man, the Count, in return for saving his man Peppino from execution.

When his band kidnaps Albert, the Count comes to the catacombs and Vampa releases him at once, apologizing. He reads Caesar's Commentaries, admires courage, keeps his word like a gentleman, and would punish any man who knowingly harmed the Count's friend.
The Count explains that he met Vampa as a shepherd boy more than ten years ago, later captured him and his band, and freed them on condition that they always respect him and his friends.
The Count enters a racehorse in Paris under the name 'Vampa', which gives him away to Albert.
He still leads his band from the catacombs of Saint Sebastian, now reading Plutarch's Life of Alexander. Danglars is led to him as a prisoner.

He answers to a higher chief who has forbidden him to shed Danglars' blood. He demands the banker's whole five million as ransom, charged meal by meal, and reminds him that some men suffered worse, dying of hunger.

A short, brutal-looking man, he rages when his fellow prisoner Peppino is pardoned, crying that he will not die alone, and is clubbed and stabbed to death.

tagline.text: Witty Venetian countess who thinks the pale Count is a vampire

description.text: A witty, beautiful Venetian aristocrat whom Franz knew in Paris. Imaginative and superstitious, she is frightened by the pale stranger at the theatre in Rome and calls him a vampire.
She later decides the Count is merely an eccentric millionaire, and teases Albert about his Carnival romance.
At the Duke of Bracciano's ball she shares the duke's unease that Albert is out in the streets at night; once rescued, he arrives to dance with her.
Now in Paris, she is unnerved when the Count's racing cup is sent to her with a note from 'Lord Ruthven', and fears he holds a grudge over her vampire jokes.
She still believes the Count is Lord Ruthven, the vampire of the stories.

description.text: An exquisitely beautiful young woman in Greek dress who has attended every performance in Rome this season and delights in the ballet. No one knows who she is; she comes with the pale stranger in the box or with a black servant.
She seems to live in the Count’s apartments: Albert and Franz hear the sound of her guzla, a stringed instrument, but never see her.
In Paris, the Count says he bought her in Constantinople, that she speaks only modern Greek, and that everyone around him is free to leave him.
