description.text: A shepherd condemned to the guillotine for supplying food to Vampa's band. Franz overhears the cloaked Count promise Vampa to save him.

A handsome, sunburned man of twenty-four or twenty-five, he walks to the scaffold with a firm step, watching for his rescuer, and is pardoned at the last moment; afterwards he slips away into the crowd.
Now serving as Vampa's messenger and fiercely grateful to the Count, he brings the ransom letter for Albert and guides the Count to the catacombs.
Albert guesses that the 'life of a man' the Pope granted the Count in exchange for an emerald was Peppino's.
Years later he shadows Danglars through Rome and leads him into the catacombs; the bandits, helped by a clerk at Thomson & French, knew in advance what the banker would draw.
An epicure who speaks perfect French, he runs the bandits' 'fixed-price' menu with flawless politeness, charging Danglars 100,000 francs for a chicken or a loaf of bread.
He keeps selling Danglars food and drink at ruinous prices, and finally ignores his pleas.

moments.text: Was pardoned at the foot of the scaffold.
Delivered the ransom letter and guided the Count to the catacombs.
Shadowed Danglars through Rome and led him into the catacombs.
Charged Danglars 100,000 francs for a fowl, or for a loaf of bread.

aliases.name: Giovanni Bertuccio
aliases.note: his full name

tagline.text: The Count of Monte Cristo's steward.
The Count's Corsican steward, haunted by a vendetta killing at Auteuil.
The steward who recognizes three figures from his past at Auteuil.
The Count's steward and Benedetto's foster-father.

description.text: Bertuccio is the Count's steward, a man of forty-five to fifty. He looks exactly like the smuggler who led Franz into the cave on Monte Cristo, but shows no sign of recognizing him.

A Corsican, he has been a soldier and a smuggler and has perhaps been in trouble with the police over ‘a stab with a knife’. He is fiercely efficient, but goes pale at the name Auteuil and tries to talk his master out of buying a house there.

He confessed to the Abbé Busoni in prison at Nîmes and was recommended to the Count by him. In the garden at Auteuil he breaks down and admits that he took a vendetta there: his victim was Villefort, who had just buried a child.

A smuggler from Rogliano raised by his older brother, he swore vengeance when Villefort refused to pursue his brother's murderer. He stabbed Villefort in the Auteuil garden and saved the newborn Villefort was burying. His sister-in-law Assunta raised the boy, Benedetto, who grew up wicked. Later he witnessed Caderousse's sale of the diamond at the inn near Beaucaire.

Wrongly arrested for the murders at the inn, he was saved by the Abbé Busoni. Returning to Corsica, he found that Benedetto had tortured Assunta and fled. He sees his misfortunes as punishment, and calls the Villeforts ‘an accursed race’.

He transforms the Auteuil house, leaving only the red room untouched. At the dinner he recognizes Madame Danglars as the woman of the garden, Villefort as the man he thought he had killed, and Andrea Cavalcanti as Benedetto.
The Count has him follow Madame Danglars, then sends him, gladly, to Normandy to prepare a house, a boat and relays of horses.
The Count says Bertuccio is alone in the world and that he holds his life in his hands. He turns pale whenever Benedetto is mentioned.

He recognized Benedetto long ago on the Champs-Élysées. He visits him in prison, warns him he has fallen into terrible hands, forbids him to claim the Count as his father, and promises to tell him his real father's name.

moments.text: Broke down in the Auteuil garden and admitted to a killing there.
Stabbed Villefort and revived the newborn child buried in a box.
Was arrested, covered in La Carconte's blood, for the murder of the jeweller.
Bought Danglars' horses for the Count for 32,000 francs.
Recognized Madame Danglars, Villefort and Andrea (Benedetto) at the Auteuil dinner.
Visited Benedetto in prison and promised to tell him his father's name.

tagline.text: Teenage bandit who lured Albert into Vampa's trap

description.text: A fifteen-year-old member of Vampa's band who disguised himself as a peasant girl and lured Albert into the ambush.

tagline.text: Roman duke famous for his balls

description.text: A Roman duke whose house is one of the most delightful in Rome; his duchess, a Colonna heiress, gives fêtes famous across Europe. At his ball he worries about Albert being out in the streets at night.

tagline.text: Albert’s friend, a quick-witted journalist on an opposition newspaper.
Newspaper editor challenged by Albert over the Yanina article.
The journalist who proved Morcerf’s treason and offered to keep it secret.

description.text: One of Albert’s friends, a journalist on an opposition paper who trades friendly political insults with Debray and is always rushing off to the Chamber of Deputies.
Sceptical by trade, he tries to catch the Count out, then decides the Count is a better story than any speech.
A cynical philosopher at heart, he doubts the Marquise de Saint-Méran really died of apoplexy.

As editor of l’Impartial, he refuses to retract the paragraph about Yanina under Albert’s threats, though he did not write it. He asks for three weeks to investigate, after which he will retract or fight.
He has secretly been to Yanina and back and found the story true. Generously, he hands Albert the only proofs to destroy and promises to keep the secret.
When another paper names Morcerf, he alerts Albert and watches the Chamber of Peers hearing from a hidden gallery.
He reveals that the banker in Yanina said Danglars had already made inquiries there, and tries to keep Albert prudent.
He apologizes on his own account for Albert’s insult at the Opera, then arranges the duel and serves as one of Albert’s seconds.
Baffled by Albert’s apology, he advises him with thin irony to leave France for a few years.
His newspaper hints that Villefort would have investigated the deaths in his house more closely had they happened elsewhere.

moments.text: Gave the Count’s bravery twenty lines in his newspaper.
Agreed to a duel with Albert after three weeks.
Gave Albert the proofs of his father’s guilt to destroy.
Sent Albert’s valet galloping to Normandy with the news.
Watched Morcerf’s hearing in secret from a gallery.
Acted as Albert’s second at the duel that ended in an apology.

tagline.text: Albert de Morcerf’s trusted valet.

description.text: Albert’s trusted valet, who runs his small household with an English groom named John, and announces the Count’s arrival at Albert’s breakfast.

aliases.name: Madame de Nargonne
aliases.note: the widow Danglars married, as Caderousse told it in ch 27

aliases.name: Baroness Danglars
aliases.note: her title

aliases.name: Hermine
aliases.note: her first name

aliases.name: Hermine de Servières
aliases.note: her maiden name (also given as de Servieux)

tagline.text: Danglars' wife, a fashionable Paris baroness.
Danglars' elegant, scornful wife, escorted to the opera by Debray.
Danglars' elegant, scornful wife, who gambles on the stock market with Debray's tips.
A baroness with a buried past: the pregnant woman Bertuccio saw with Villefort.
Mother of Villefort's lost child, who learns the baby may have lived.
Abandoned by husband and lover, she is left alone but rich.
Benedetto's mother, recognized when she collapsed at his trial.

description.text: Madame Danglars is the banker's wife, the widow Madame de Nargonne whom Danglars married. She moves in the best Paris circles and sends Albert de Morcerf a perfumed note offering him a seat in her opera box.

Danglars boasts that she comes from an ancient family, born de Servières, and that her first husband was the Marquis de Nargonne. The Count seems to know more about the couple's private life than he lets on.

Still handsome, she has refined taste, a temper, and open contempt for her husband. She is close to Lucien Debray, the minister's secretary, and to Madame de Villefort. She is furious to find her beloved dappled grays sold behind her back.

Debray is openly her lover. She is a daring, willful speculator on the stock exchange, using Debray's inside knowledge of government news to steer her husband's investments. She is eager to meet the Count and to be invited to his house.

At the Count's dinner at Auteuil, Bertuccio recognizes her as the young, pregnant widow he saw years ago in that very garden, waiting for Villefort, on the night Villefort buried a newborn child there. She looks anxiously over the house from the moment she arrives.
Every hint the Count drops about the red room, the hidden staircase and a child shakes her more, until she faints.

Her husband reveals he has known about her affairs for sixteen years, including her past with Villefort, and has tolerated them for his own profit. She has made 500,000 livres this year from Debray's tips. Her first husband, M. de Nargonne, is said to have died of grief or rage on coming home after nine months away to find her six months pregnant.

Veiled, she secretly visits Villefort. As M. de Nargonne's widow she bore Villefort's child in the red damask room at Auteuil and was told it was born dead; she has mourned it ever since. Villefort tells her the child may have survived, and she is both overjoyed and horrified.
Still nervous of the Count but charmed whenever he appears, she claims to have given up speculating.
She proudly announces Eugénie's coming marriage to ‘Prince’ Cavalcanti.

After Andrea's arrest she fears her clever daughter, who despises her affair and money dealings with Debray. She uses her old intimacy with Villefort to beg him to let Benedetto escape or delay his trial, but he refuses.
Abandoned by Danglars, she hopes Debray will protect her. Instead he coolly hands over her share of their joint speculations, and she leaves him without a farewell, rich in money but humiliated.
She attends Benedetto's trial veiled. When he declares that his mother believed him born dead, she cries out and collapses, her veil falls, and she is recognized.

moments.text: Discovered her dappled grays had been sold and harnessed to the Count's carriage.
Fainted when the Count imagined a man carrying a sleeping child down the hidden staircase.
Turned white when her husband named Villefort among those who ‘trembled’ before him.
Secretly visited Villefort and learned their child might still be alive.
Begged Villefort to let Benedetto escape, or at least delay his trial, and was refused.
Took her 1,340,000 francs and walked out on Debray without a farewell.
Fainted at Benedetto's trial and was carried out of the courtroom.

tagline.text: Albert’s cool, witty friend, private secretary to the Minister of the Interior.
The minister’s secretary, Madame Danglars’ lover and stock-market tipster.
Madame Danglars’ former lover, who left her coldly once she was of no use.

description.text: A tall, fair, cool young man, private secretary to the Minister of the Interior. Witty and worldly, he is one of Albert’s friends.
He doubts the Count exists, then promises to find out through the ministry’s police who the man really is.
He is a frequent and very much at-home visitor to Madame Danglars, whose boudoir they decorated together; her husband treats this as normal.
He lets slip that it is Madame Danglars who gambles on the stock market, and is embarrassed when Albert jokes about feeding her government news.
As the minister’s secretary he sees official telegraph news first, and passes it straight to Madame Danglars.
He is plainly Madame Danglars’ lover. Danglars accuses him of pocketing the money she made from his inside tips.
Friends urge him to marry Eugénie for her money, an idea he half likes but knows is hopeless.

He and Madame Danglars have been secret partners in speculation, turning her 100,000 francs into millions. Once she is no longer useful, he pays her share and drops her coldly, keeping over a million francs for himself.

moments.text: Arrived first at Albert’s breakfast, after a night writing dispatches.
Rushed to tell the baroness that her husband must sell his Spanish bonds.
Was coolly dismissed from Madame Danglars’ rooms by her husband.
Paid Madame Danglars her share and let her go without a kind word.

tagline.text: Albert’s well-born friend, a duellist and amateur soldier.

description.text: A handsome, well-born gentleman of about thirty in Albert’s circle. He once wounded Franz d’Épinay in a duel and went to Algeria to fight “as an amateur.” He judges the Count to be a great man.
A fine horseman with a sharp eye, he is a regular at society gatherings and remarks on everyone.
He is one of Franz’s witnesses for the marriage contract.
He backs Albert without question in his quarrel with the count and agrees to act as one of his seconds.
At the duel he is stunned by Albert’s apology, which he finds either very despicable or very noble.
He instinctively dislikes Madame de Villefort.
He remarks that Morcerf’s pistol shot seems kinder than Villefort’s public ruin.

moments.text: Spread the story of the Count’s bravery at the Jockey Club.
Acted as Albert’s second at the duel.

aliases.name: Claire-Marie-Eugénie Danglars
aliases.note: her full name

aliases.name: Léon d'Armilly
aliases.note: the name she travels under, disguised as a young man

tagline.text: Danglars' daughter, talked of as Albert de Morcerf's future bride.
Danglars' proud, gifted daughter, cold toward her intended, Albert.
Engaged by her father to Andrea Cavalcanti, a match she merely tolerates.
Fled Paris disguised as a young man, to live as an artist.

description.text: Eugénie is Danglars' daughter, spoken of as Albert de Morcerf's intended bride, with a dowry of two million francs. Albert's friends doubt the proud Morcerfs will ever accept a banker's daughter.

Handsome and severe, with black hair and eyes and a habitual frown. She is a gifted linguist, artist and musician. She treats Albert coolly and is frank to the point of rudeness: she bluntly asks the Count whether Haydée is his daughter.

Still only seventeen, she dislikes the idea of marrying Albert and prizes her independence; she almost wishes her father would lose his fortune so that she could live as an artist. She makes music every day with her friend Louise d'Armilly.

Her father now prefers Andrea Cavalcanti as a son-in-law. Cold, beautiful and satirical, she ignores Andrea's sighs, though the two are admired singing together. Albert says the two of them regard each other with mutual indifference.
She put up with Andrea only to be rid of Albert, and now openly dislikes him.

She tells her father she loves no one, wants no husband, and believes she could earn a fortune as a singer. She agrees to sign the marriage contract in three days only on condition that she remains entirely free, and keeps her own plans to herself.

Scornful of all men, she had planned to run away even before Andrea was exposed. That night she cuts off her hair, dresses as a man, and leaves Paris as ‘Léon d'Armilly’ with Louise, meaning to live as an artist in Italy.
At an inn in Compiègne, Andrea falls into their room; she coldly urges him to kill himself, then has to leave through a jeering crowd.

moments.text: Bluntly asked the Count whether Haydée was his daughter.
Agreed to sign the marriage contract, on her own terms.
Fled Paris disguised as a young man.
Urged Andrea to kill himself rather than be taken.

tagline.text: Bertuccio's kind, widowed sister-in-law, who raised the foundling Benedetto.

description.text: Assunta is Bertuccio's widowed sister-in-law in Rogliano, Corsica. A kind woman, she secretly reclaimed the baby Bertuccio had left at the foundling hospital, named him Benedetto, raised him as her own and spoiled him.
Benedetto and two companions held her over the fire to make her give up her money. She was found terribly burned and died.

moments.text: Died after being burned by Benedetto and his friends.

tagline.text: The baby Bertuccio rescued from Villefort's garden, raised in Corsica.
Bertuccio's wicked foster-son, who tortured Assunta and vanished.

description.text: Benedetto is the newborn child that Bertuccio, in his story to the Count, saw Villefort bury in a box in the garden at Auteuil. Having stabbed Villefort, Bertuccio dug up the baby and revived it. Its fine linen was marked with an H and an N under a baron's coronet. He left the child at a Paris foundling hospital, but his widowed sister-in-law Assunta reclaimed it, named it Benedetto, and raised it in Corsica.

Blond, clever and spoiled by Assunta, the boy grew up a liar and a thief. He knew Bertuccio was not his father, was running with older criminals by the age of eleven, and laughed at Bertuccio's plan to send him to sea.
While Bertuccio was away, Benedetto and two companions held Assunta over the fire to make her give up her money, robbed the house and disappeared. Bertuccio hopes he is dead.

moments.text: Was buried alive at birth by Villefort and rescued by Bertuccio.
Mocked Bertuccio's offer to take him to sea.
Tortured his foster-mother Assunta for money and disappeared.

tagline.text: Bertuccio's elder brother, murdered in Nîmes in 1815.

description.text: Bertuccio's older brother, who raised him, was a lieutenant in a Corsican regiment of Napoleon's army. He was murdered in Nîmes in 1815 during the royalist massacres, and Villefort's refusal to seek justice set off Bertuccio's vendetta.

aliases.name: Johannes
aliases.note: spelling used when the abbé recalls the murder

tagline.text: Paris jeweller who buys Caderousse's diamond.
The jeweller murdered at Caderousse's inn.

description.text: Joannes is a jeweller from the Palais Royal in Paris who bargains Caderousse's diamond down to 45,000 francs. Armed with pistols, he returns to the inn to shelter from a storm.
He is murdered in his bed at the inn, after fighting back with his pistols.

moments.text: Was stabbed to death at Caderousse's inn.

tagline.text: The lovely young Greek woman who lives secluded in the Count’s house.
The Count’s Greek ward, who accuses Morcerf of betraying her father.
Daughter of Ali Pasha of Yanina, sold into slavery and freed by the Count.
Ali Pasha’s daughter, whose testimony brought down the Count de Morcerf.
Ali Pasha’s daughter, who chose to stay with the count out of love.

description.text: Haydée is the beautiful Greek woman glimpsed with the Count in Rome. She arrives at his Paris house at midnight, kisses his hand with love and respect, and is given hidden apartments, kept apart from the French servants.
The Count speaks of her as his slave.

About nineteen or twenty, from Epirus, she is devoted to the Count. She has loved only her late father, a white-bearded man of about sixty, and the Count — and she says her love for him is not a daughter’s. Told she is free, she refuses ever to leave him. He asks her to keep the secret of her birth.

At the Opera she dazzles the audience, then nearly faints on seeing the Count de Morcerf. When told he served her father, she cries that he sold her father to the Turks and that his fortune was the price of that treachery. Since Morcerf served Ali Pasha of Yanina, it seems her father was Ali himself.
The count tells Mercédès she is a prince’s daughter he bought as a slave in Constantinople and has adopted, having no one else to love.

She tells Albert her story: she is the daughter of Ali Tepelini, Pasha of Yanina, and his wife Vasiliki. When she was four, her father was betrayed by a French officer he trusted and killed by the sultan’s troops. She and her mother were sold as slaves, and after her mother’s death she passed through other hands until the count acquired her.

She has always meant to avenge her father and follows every newspaper in her seclusion. Without telling the count, she appears before the Chamber of Peers with her birth records and the bill of sale proving that Fernand Mondego sold her and her mother, and denounces Morcerf to his face.
Afraid for the count before his duel, she waits all night outside his door; on reading his will she tears it up, saying she will need nothing if he dies.
She greets the count with a joy that seems both a daughter’s and a lover’s.
She leaves Paris ahead of the count to wait for him.
The count offers to free her and restore her father’s name and wealth, but she says she would die without him, loving him “as one loves a father, brother, husband.”

moments.text: Arrived at the Count’s Paris house at midnight.
Promised the Count she would never leave him.
Recognized the Count de Morcerf at the Opera and denounced him as the man who betrayed her father.
Told Albert the story of her father’s betrayal and death.
Testified before the Chamber of Peers and denounced Morcerf to his face.
Tore up the count’s will.
Declared her love for the count and sailed away with him.

tagline.text: The Count's discreet French valet in Paris

description.text: The Count's French valet, in his service for a year. He is warned never to gossip about his master and told that loyal servants share a fund to be divided at the Count's death.
Efficient and perfectly discreet, he has orders to admit no one but Major Cavalcanti and his son. Albert would love to employ him.
He recognizes the major from his master's exact description and shows him in.
He is sharply rebuked for questioning orders when he delivers an anonymous warning letter.
He follows his master to the duel with Albert in terror.
He is the only servant who leaves Paris with the Count and Morrel.

moments.text: Recognized the Cavalcanti visitors from the Count's description.
Delivered the anonymous warning letter and was rebuked for questioning orders.
Left Paris with the Count and Morrel, the only servant to do so.

aliases.name: Edward de Villefort
aliases.note: full name

tagline.text: Madame de Villefort's spoiled, crafty little son.
Valentine's spoiled half-brother, his mother's idol.
Villefort's young son, for whose inheritance the poisonings were committed.
Villefort's young son, poisoned by his own mother.

description.text: A small, pale boy of seven or eight with a crafty look, spoiled and willful. Revived by a drop of the Count's elixir after the carriage accident, he refuses to thank Ali because he is 'too ugly'.
Valentine's troublesome half-brother and the object of his mother's overpowering love. He tortures the parrot and mocks his sister, and is barely scolded.
He inherits nothing from Valentine's mother, so he is poor beside his half-sister. He idolizes the Count, who brings him presents.
Noirtier refuses to have him sent to his room, and refuses, with something like hatred, to leave him anything in his will.
He is still up to mischief, emptying Valentine's water decanter to make a pond for his ducks.
As Villefort's only son, he would eventually inherit Valentine's fortune, and the Count says the crimes in the house were committed on his account.
His mother, condemned by Villefort, sent for him half an hour before his father returned home. He was found dead on the sofa in her boudoir.

moments.text: Was revived by one drop of the Count's red elixir.
Blurted out, 'Grandpapa Noirtier can speak now, then?'
Was kissed and sent out of the room by his father before the confrontation with his mother.
Was found dead on a sofa in his mother's boudoir.

aliases.name: Héloïse de Villefort
aliases.note: her first name

tagline.text: Villefort's young second wife, devoted to her spoiled son Edward.
Valentine's smiling stepmother, who lives for her own son.
Valentine's stepmother, revealed as the poisoner killing so Edward will inherit.
Unmasked poisoner, ordered by her husband to take her own life.
The poisoner who died by her own hand, taking her son with her.

description.text: Villefort's young second wife, who dotes on her spoiled son Edward. After the Count saves them from runaway horses, she is fascinated by him and his case of remedies, and urges her husband to visit him.
Valentine says her stepmother hides hostility behind constant smiles, adores her own son, and has no fortune of her own.

She has long been fascinated by Mithridates and poisons, and knows a good deal of botany and chemistry. She keeps the Count talking about drugs and their effects, and asks for, and gets, the recipe for his elixir.

Valentine believes her stepmother would prefer she never married at all: if Valentine took the veil, her fortune would go to Villefort and in time to Edward. Madame de Villefort admires Monte Cristo enormously.
She hoped Noirtier would leave his fortune to Edward, and is angry when he refuses, but she cannot hide her joy that Valentine has been disinherited.
She suggests Valentine and Noirtier planned the will together, and keeps returning to how unfair it is to Edward.
When the grieving Marquise de Saint-Méran, her husband's first mother-in-law, arrives, her presence seems to distress the old lady, so she withdraws.
She surprises Noirtier by visiting him, claiming she always opposed the d'Épinay marriage, and asking him to restore his fortune to Valentine.
When Valentine feels unwell, she tells her to go and drink a glass of water, and says she fears a serious illness.

The truth comes out: she is the poisoner. She creeps through Edward's room into Valentine's at night to dose her drink. The Count says she has been plotting ever since she asked him about aqua tofana in Perugia, killing so that Edward will inherit everything.
Standing over Valentine she feels a stir of fear and remorse, but she carefully empties and rinses the glass. She faints when d'Avrigny finds poison in it anyway.

Confronted by Villefort, she cannot deny the four murders. She begs for her life for Edward's sake and laughs wildly at the idea that she could ever harm him. He orders her to take her own poison before he returns.
Believing a good mother cannot leave her son behind, she poisoned both herself and Edward, leaving a note for her husband.

moments.text: Was rescued with her son when Madame Danglars' horses bolted at Auteuil.
Asked for, and received, the recipe for the Count's elixir.
Lent the Count her smelling bottle to revive Madame Danglars.
Asked Noirtier to make Valentine his heir again.
Was seen by Valentine pouring poison into her glass at night.
Rinsed Valentine's glass before dawn, then fainted when d'Avrigny found poison in it anyway.
Was condemned by her husband and locked in to die by her own hand.
Poisoned herself and her son Edward.

aliases.name: Mademoiselle de Villefort
aliases.note: Villefort's daughter

tagline.text: A young friend of Eugénie Danglars, mentioned in a letter.
Villefort's daughter, devoted nurse of her paralyzed grandfather.
Villefort's daughter, engaged to Franz but secretly in love with Maximilian Morrel.
Villefort's daughter, freed from her engagement to Franz, hoping to marry Maximilian.
Rich young heiress whom d'Avrigny suspects of a string of poisonings.
Villefort's daughter, who collapses after drinking a bitter glass of water.
Villefort's daughter, struck down by poison and barely surviving.
Poisoning target who now knows her stepmother is trying to kill her.
Villefort's daughter, found dead in her bed.
Villefort's daughter, found dead in her bed and buried at Père-Lachaise.
Alive after all: her death was staged by the Count; reunited with Maximilian.

description.text: First mentioned in a postscript to Madame de Villefort's letter, sending her love to Eugénie Danglars.
Villefort's daughter by his first wife, nearly eighteen. She looks after her paralyzed grandfather Noirtier.

She is engaged against her will to Franz d'Épinay and in love with Maximilian Morrel, whom she meets secretly at the garden gate. Neglected by her father and, she feels, quietly hated by her stepmother, her only comfort at home is her grandfather, whose eye signals only she can read.
Tall and graceful, with chestnut hair and blue eyes, she looks sad and has been crying. She went to Italy for her health two years ago.

She is rich in her own right and expects inheritances from her grandparents, which is why her stepmother once encouraged her to become a nun. She gave up the convent only because of her grandfather's despairing look. She distrusts Monte Cristo, who seems to avoid her.
She cares nothing for money, only for her grandfather's love. She interprets his signals for the notary as he disinherits her to block the match with Franz.
After her grandfather's sudden death she nurses her grandmother through a fever, not daring to mention Maximilian because of the old lady's contempt for commoners.
Torn between duty and love, she introduces Maximilian to Noirtier and swears by her mother's memory to run away with him rather than sign the contract.
When Noirtier answers Franz's question about his father's killer, she understands first; she has often seen the two scars on her grandfather's arm.
Franz breaks off the engagement. Freed, she tells Maximilian 'We are saved!' Noirtier makes her his heir, and with the Saint-Méran fortune she can expect a huge income.

It was she who carried in the lemonade that killed Barrois. D'Avrigny points out that she handled the drinks and medicines in every case and accuses her of the poisonings, though she knows nothing of it.

Unwell for two weeks and finding everything bitter, she has been taking spoonfuls of her grandfather's medicine on his orders. After drinking a glass of water she collapses into rigid unconsciousness.
She survives a heavy dose of poison, thanks to the resistance Noirtier built up in her with his medicine.
Still weak and troubled by night visions, she is visited by Monte Cristo, who tells her that someone has been poisoning her drinks and that he has been watching over her.

She learns her stepmother is the poisoner and her fortune the motive. She would rather die than denounce her, and her first thought is fear for Edward. She takes a pill from the Count's emerald box, promising to fear nothing, even if she wakes in a tomb.
She is found cold, rigid and breathless in her bed, and Dr. d'Avrigny pronounces her dead.
Her death is officially confirmed, and after a great funeral she is buried in the Saint-Méran and Villefort vault at Père-Lachaise, mourned by a crowd of young people.

She is alive. The Count's drug let her appear dead, and she has been waiting on the island with Haydée, whom she loves as a sister. She learns from his letter that her father is mad and her brother dead, and she is reunited with Maximilian.

moments.text: Confessed her love and unhappiness to Maximilian through the garden gate.
Interpreted Noirtier's signals as he made his will.
Signalled to Maximilian across the ballroom with her bouquet of forget-me-nots.
Fainted on hearing of her grandfather's death.
Introduced Maximilian to Noirtier and declared she would be his alone.
Told Maximilian 'We are saved!' after the engagement was broken.
Was accused of the poisonings by d'Avrigny, though innocent.
Collapsed in Noirtier's room after drinking a glass of water.
Was visited at night by the Count, who told her that her drinks were poisoned.
Swallowed a pill from the Count's emerald box, promising to fear nothing.
Was found lifeless in her bed and pronounced dead.
Was buried at Père-Lachaise after a crowded funeral.
Appeared alive at Maximilian's side.

tagline.text: A Sicilian ‘terrible chemist’ the Count claims as a friend.

description.text: The Abbé Adelmonte of Taormina is a Sicilian chemist the Count tells Madame de Villefort about. He supposedly showed how poison passed along a chain of animals could kill without trace, leaving only signs of apoplexy, and is said to have made the Count's elixir.

tagline.text: Eugénie Danglars' schoolfriend, a talented young singer without fortune.
Eugénie's companion in her flight from Paris.

description.text: Louise d'Armilly is a talented young singer without fortune, a schoolfellow of Eugénie Danglars who practices music with her every day. Because Louise is destined for the stage, Eugénie takes care never to be seen with her in public.
Small, delicate and fairy-like, she is Eugénie's singing teacher and confidante, often staying at the Danglars house, and will not say a word to Albert.
She is going to Italy, and the Count has given her letters of introduction to theatre directors there.
Timid but devoted, she bought the post-chaise and keeps the money for Eugénie's flight, and travels with her, posing as her sister.
When Andrea falls into their room at the inn in Compiègne, she rings for help, then pities him and urges him to escape.

moments.text: Thanked the Count for her letters of introduction, saying she meant to use them at once.
Escaped from Paris with Eugénie.

description.text: Andrea is the son of the Italian nobleman Major Cavalcanti, described by the Count as a charming young man of about Albert's age. He is about to enter Paris society backed by his father's millions, and the Count has promised to keep an eye on him.

The story goes that he was stolen from his father at the age of five. He is tall, with light hair, a red beard and black eyes, quick-witted and a fluent liar who reads legal papers like an expert. In fact he is a hired player: promised 50,000 livres a year to act as the major's son, he starts in fear at the news of his ‘father’, and the Count hints that his youth was ‘stormy’.

At the dinner at Auteuil, Bertuccio recognizes him on sight: ‘Andrea Cavalcanti’ is Benedetto. He is the newborn that Villefort buried alive in that garden, and that Bertuccio, after stabbing Villefort, dug up and revived. The baby was left at a foundling hospital, reclaimed by Bertuccio's widowed sister-in-law Assunta, and raised in Corsica.

There the clever, spoiled boy became a liar and a thief who ran with criminals by eleven. In the end, with two companions, he held Assunta over the fire for her money, robbed the house and vanished. At the same dinner Bertuccio recognizes Madame Danglars as the pregnant woman he saw waiting for Villefort in the garden that night.

Leaving the dinner, he is ambushed by Caderousse, who knew him in the past as Benedetto. Andrea says he was brought up in Corsica, and agrees to pay Caderousse 200 francs a month to keep quiet. He carries a pistol, and was alarmed to find the king's prosecutor at the table.

Within a fortnight he is accepted everywhere, rumored heir to the Saravezza quarries and flattered by Danglars as ‘Prince’. Vain and polished, though his low birth shows through, he openly courts Eugénie with her father's blessing, while the Count pointedly refuses to vouch for him.

He proposes to Eugénie and is accepted. Caderousse was his comrade in the galleys at Toulon, and they escaped together. Andrea claims to believe the Count is his real father and has left him money in his will. Under pressure from Caderousse, he draws him a plan of the Count's house and tells him when it will be empty.

Caught breaking into the Count's house, Caderousse tells the abbé that Andrea is Benedetto, a Corsican foundling and convict No. 59. Climbing down from the wall, Caderousse is stabbed. Before he dies he says Benedetto gave him the plan hoping one would kill the other, then lay in wait, and signs a deposition naming him as the murderer.

Boastful and greedy, he frets over the dowry and the three million. At the signing of the marriage contract, when the Count tells of Caderousse's bloodstained waistcoat and a letter found in it, he slips away just before police arrive to arrest him.

Without remorse and full of resource, he steals jewels from the wedding presents and nearly escapes through the chimneys, but is trapped at an inn in Compiègne, falling into the room of Eugénie and Louise. Cornered, he refuses to kill himself, saying ‘one has friends’, and is taken to prison in Paris.
Villefort, preparing the case, describes him as a Corsican vagabond of unknown parents, sent to the galleys at sixteen for forgery, who escaped and is now accused of murder.

In prison he still poses as a Cavalcanti prince, sure a powerful protector will save him, and suspects the Count is his father. Bertuccio, his ‘adopted father’, visits and warns him he has fallen into terrible hands, promising to tell him his true father's name.

At his trial he declares that he was born at Auteuil, the son of the prosecutor M. de Villefort, who buried him alive, and that his mother believed him born dead. Rescued, left at a foundling hospital and raised in Corsica, he has no name of his own and blames his father for everything he became.

description.text: The Count describes Major Cavalcanti as a polite, modest Italian nobleman of very ancient family whom he met in Florence, Bologna and Lucca.

In reality he is a man of about fifty-two in shabby, old-fashioned clothes who barely knows the story he is supposed to tell: that he is a rich noble of Lucca and former Austrian major whose son was stolen as a child. He is paid 50,000 francs to play the father, cares mainly about the money, and agrees with Andrea to play the game to the end without asking who is behind it.

Dressed in a major's uniform covered with medals, he looks every inch the old soldier and wisely says little at the Count's dinner. He turns his banknotes into a large diamond ring, and Danglars, dazzled, opens an account for him and his son.
His part played, he leaves Paris and goes back to gambling at the baths of Lucca, leaving Andrea the family papers.
Letters in his name approve Andrea's marriage from Parma, regret that he cannot leave, and promise a wedding gift of 150,000 livres.
He does not come to the contract signing; a representative signs for him.

moments.text: Received 8,000 francs on account and was told his ‘lost son’ Andrea was waiting in the next room.
Admitted to Andrea that he was paid to play his father.
Innocently asked at dinner what is done to child-murderers in France.
Cashed a 40,000-franc bond with Danglars and opened a monthly allowance for his son.

tagline.text: Noirtier's faithful old servant, loyal to no other master.
Noirtier's devoted servant, who died after drinking his master's lemonade.

description.text: Noirtier's servant of twenty-five years, who recognizes no master but Noirtier and anticipates his every wish, ignoring Villefort when he must.
He guards Noirtier's door and shows Maximilian out by a hidden passage.
With unusual firmness he announces to the assembled family that Noirtier demands to see Franz at once.
He alone knows the secret spring of his master's old writing desk, and opens it to bring out the record of General d'Épinay's death.
About sixty, he made Noirtier's lemonade and left it in the pantry. Hot and thirsty, he drank a glass and died in convulsions.
D'Avrigny says he died in another's place, poisoned by a dose meant for his master, but publicly gives the cause as apoplexy.

moments.text: Went off to fetch a notary for his master despite Villefort's objections.

description.text: Franz d'Épinay's father, assassinated in 1815; his killers were never found. He and Noirtier were bitter political enemies.

He was General de Quesnel, created Baron d'Épinay, who served under Napoleon but kept royalist sympathies. He was killed one evening after leaving a Bonapartist meeting he had been invited to, the same disappearance the police were investigating in 1815. Villefort calls him a friend.

Noirtier's signed record tells the truth: invited to the Bonapartist club, the general refused to break his oath to Louis XVIII, was made to swear silence, then insulted the club's president, Noirtier. They fought a fair duel on the Quai des Ormes on 5 February 1815; the general was killed and his body thrown into the river.

moments.text: Was revealed to have died in a duel with Noirtier, not by assassination.

description.text: The Villefort family notary, who takes charge of Noirtier's sealed will.
He presides over the signing of Valentine's marriage contract and tells Franz about Noirtier's will.

moments.text: Presided over the interrupted signing of Valentine's marriage contract.

tagline.text: Gentle signal-tower operator whom the Count bribes to send false news.

description.text: A poor, gentle man of fifty-five who has worked the Montlhéry signal tower for fifteen years at 1,000 francs a year. He loves his tiny garden and his war on the dormice, and repeats signals without understanding them. The Count pays him to send a false message.

moments.text: Sent the Count's false signals, then fainted with emotion.

tagline.text: Madame Danglars' late first husband.

description.text: M. de Nargonne was Madame Danglars' first husband. According to Danglars, he died of grief or rage when he came home after nine months away and found his wife six months pregnant.
He was a baron, which explains the baron's coronet over the letter H (for Hermine) on her linen.

description.text: Mademoiselle Cornélie is Madame Danglars' trusted maid.

tagline.text: Trieste banker whose failure costs Danglars about a million francs.

description.text: Jacopo Manfredi is a banker of Trieste, long a reliable client of Danglars, who has suspended payments and cost him about a million francs.

tagline.text: The Villeforts' family doctor and old friend.
Family doctor who suspects poison in the Villefort house but agrees to keep quiet.
Family doctor who pronounced Valentine dead and found poison in her glass.

description.text: A brilliant doctor and old friend of the family who was present at Valentine's birth. He has a daughter, Madeleine. He finds the marquise's symptoms strange.

He is convinced Madame de Saint-Méran died of brucine or strychnine, poisons that mimic tetanus; he has been giving Noirtier brucine as treatment. He agrees to keep silent but warns Villefort that the evil may not stop.
When Barrois dies, he questions everyone and proves with syrup of violets that the lemonade was poisoned, linking the death to the marquise's.

He believes the poison was meant for Noirtier, protected by his brucine treatment, and accuses Valentine because she gains from every death. When Villefort refuses to act, he agrees to keep silent but vows never to return to the house.
He comes back when Valentine collapses, is astonished she survives, and works out how Noirtier has been protecting her. He orders that no one give her anything without his instructions.
He declares Valentine dead and, testing her drink, identifies a new poison.
He regrets that his earlier silence encouraged the murderer, but at Villefort's plea agrees to keep the secret and arranges the formalities.

moments.text: Agreed to stay silent about the poisoning but warned Villefort to watch carefully.
Proved Barrois had been poisoned.
Accused Valentine of the poisonings, then withdrew from the house.
Returned to treat Valentine and took charge of everything she drank.
Declared Valentine dead and found poison in her glass.

tagline.text: The sultan’s commander sent to capture Ali Pasha.

description.text: The Seraskier Kourchid was the sultan’s commander sent against Ali Pasha. His soldiers killed Selim and Ali, and he handed Vasiliki and Haydée over to their new master.

tagline.text: Ali Pasha’s faithful soldier, who guarded his gold and gunpowder.

description.text: Ali Pasha’s favourite soldier, who guarded a cavern of gold and gunpowder with a lit match, ready to blow it all up on Ali’s signal. He was stabbed as soon as he put out the match.
Haydée accuses Morcerf of having stabbed him.

moments.text: Put out the match on seeing Ali’s ring and was murdered.

tagline.text: Haydée’s mother, Ali Pasha’s beloved Christian wife.

description.text: Haydée’s mother and Ali Pasha’s beloved wife, a Christian. After Ali’s death she was handed over to the man most responsible for it, sold to slave merchants, and died at the gates of Constantinople at the sight of Ali’s head.
The bill of sale shown to the Chamber of Peers proves that she and Haydée were sold together by Fernand Mondego.

moments.text: Died in Constantinople at the sight of her husband’s head.

description.text: Albert’s valet, who rides fifteen hours to bring him Beauchamp’s letter and the newspaper naming his father.

moments.text: Brought Albert the news of the second article.

tagline.text: The slave merchant who bought Haydée and her mother from Fernand.

description.text: A slave merchant who supplied the sultan’s harem. His document records buying Vasiliki and Haydée from Fernand Mondego for 400,000 francs, and Haydée’s later purchase by the Count of Monte Cristo for an emerald.
